CT-SAC vs PHAST control comparison on Windy Environments

William Earthman1,

1Oden Institute, UT Austin

Paper arXiv Code Interactive demo Data
TL;DR

We created three windy environments to test a suite of RL and PHAST-type control algorithms on. These environments are integrated using stochastic heun method. They are stochastic counterparts to the inverted pendulum, acrobot, and cartpole.

Abstract

Control benchmarks are usually deterministic, which lets a controller succeed by being accurate. Adding process noise changes the problem: the target must be held against continual forcing, and accuracy alone stops being sufficient. — one more sentence on why that gap matters for the model-based vs model-free question.

We introduce three stochastic ("windy") continuous-time environments — pendulum, cart-pole and acrobot — integrated with a stochastic Heun scheme under state-dependent wind σ(p)=σgust+λturb∣p∣/I\sigma(p) = \sigma_\text{gust} + \lambda_\text{turb}|p|/Iσ(p)=σgust​+λturb​∣p∣/I. — say what makes them a benchmark rather than three one-off envs (shared metric, shared plant interface, difficulty knob).

Third paragraph: what you ran on them and the one finding you would defend — the success/effort split between CT-SAC and the Casimir oracle — plus the caveat that the q-only Casimir peer is not yet in the table.

Setup

The system under study

Our first environment is the windy inverted pendulum. The control goal in this environment is to stabilize the pendulum at the unstable equilibrium of θ=π\theta = \piθ=π for a specific length of time. We characterize stabilization by being under a specific distance in phase space from upright for an alloted time period.

θ˙=pI,p˙=−mgLsin⁡θ  −  D(θ) pI  +  u\dot\theta = \frac{p}{I}, \qquad \dot p = -mgL\sin\theta \;-\; D(\theta)\,\frac{p}{I} \;+\; uθ˙=Ip​,p˙​=−mgLsinθ−D(θ)Ip​+u

The equations above are our determinstic equations of motion. We add wind into the momentum equation by

dp=(−mglsin⁡(θ)−D(θ)pI+u)dt+σ(p)∘dWtdp = (-mgl \sin(\theta) - \frac{D(\theta) p}{I} + u)dt + \sigma(p) \circ dW_tdp=(−mglsin(θ)−ID(θ)p​+u)dt+σ(p)∘dWt​
, where σ(p)\sigma(p)σ(p) is a momentum dependent wind and dWtdW_tdWt​ is Brownian noise injected at each time step. Where σ(p)=σgust+λturb∣p∣I.\sigma(p) = \sigma_{gust}+\lambda_{turb} \frac{|p|}{I}.σ(p)=σgust​+λturb​I∣p∣​. We integrate using Stratonovich on Wong-Zakai grounds.

Other environments

Our remaining two windy environments are the cartpole, and acrobot. They are integrated in a similar way. The acrobot's dynamics are built using Hamilton's equations dq=∂H∂pdq = \frac{\partial H}{\partial p}dq=∂p∂H​ and dp=∂H∂q−d(θ)+udp= \frac{\partial H}{\partial q} - d(\theta) + udp=∂q∂H​−d(θ)+u, where torque is only applied to the actuated joint. So we use a similar stochastic Heun scheme where

    • What the uncontrolled plant does

    Before introducing any controller it is worth seeing the problem the controllers face. The open-loop system (u=0u = 0u=0) has two equilibria: hanging at φ=±π\varphi = \pm\piφ=±π is a stable spiral, and upright at φ=0\varphi = 0φ=0 is a saddle. Every trajectory that is not on the saddle's stable manifold is carried away from upright and spirals into the hanging well. Stabilising upright therefore means holding the system at an equilibrium the dynamics actively reject — and the wind supplies a continual push off the stable manifold.

    Method

    The two controllers

    Energy-Casimir Controller CT-SAC Controller

    Energy-Casimir controller

    The plant above is port-Hamiltonian: writing x=(θ,p)x = (\theta, p)x=(θ,p) and H(x)=p22I−mgLcos⁡θH(x) = \tfrac{p^2}{2I} - mgL\cos\thetaH(x)=2Ip2​−mgLcosθ, its deterministic dynamics take the form x˙=(J−R)∇H(x)+Gu\dot x = (J - R)\nabla H(x) + Gux˙=(J−R)∇H(x)+Gu with JJJ skew-symmetric and R⪰0R \succeq 0R⪰0 carrying the damping D(θ)D(\theta)D(θ). Energy-Casimir control exploits that structure directly: rather than cancelling the physics and imposing a desired response, we attach a second port-Hamiltonian system — the controller — through a power-preserving interconnection, and shape the combined energy so that its minimum sits at the target.

    The controller state here is a single virtual position ξ\xiξ driven by the plant velocity. Under the interconnection, the quantity C(x,ξ)=ξ−θC(x,\xi) = \xi - \thetaC(x,ξ)=ξ−θ is conserved along closed-loop trajectories: it is a Casimir, a function the interconnection structure cannot change. That is what makes the method work — because ξ\xiξ and θ\thetaθ are locked together up to a constant, a potential built on ξ\xiξ acts on the plant coordinate, and we may add it to the plant energy to form the Lyapunov candidate

    Hcl(x,ξ)  =  Hp(x)+Hc(ξ)=Hp(x)+12kc(ξ−q⋆)2.H_{cl}(x, \xi) \;=\; H_p(x) + H_c(\xi)= H_p(x) + \tfrac{1}{2}k_c(\xi - q^\star)^2 .Hcl​(x,ξ)=Hp​(x)+Hc​(ξ)=Hp​(x)+21​kc​(ξ−q⋆)2.

    Shaping the potential fixes where the closed loop comes to rest; it does not make it settle. Injecting damping on the passive output supplies the dissipation, giving the control law

    u  =  −kc(ξ−q⋆)⏟energy shaping  − Dinj q˙^⏟damping injection,ξ˙  =  q˙^  +  kξ (θ−ξ),u \;=\; \underbrace{-k_c(\xi - q^\star)}_{\text{energy shaping}} \;\underbrace{-\,D_\text{inj}\,\hat{\dot q}}_{\text{damping injection}}, \qquad \dot\xi \;=\; \hat{\dot q} \;+\; k_\xi\,(\theta - \xi),u=energy shaping−kc​(ξ−q⋆)​​damping injection−Dinj​q˙​^​​​,ξ˙​=q˙​^​+kξ​(θ−ξ),

    where q⋆=πq^\star = \piq⋆=π is the upright target and q˙^\hat{\dot q}q˙​^​ is the velocity estimate. The first term of ξ˙\dot\xiξ˙​ is the Casimir coupling proper. The second, weighted by kξk_\xikξ​, is a predictor–corrector that is not part of the conservative structure: integrating q˙^\hat{\dot q}q˙​^​ alone lets ξ\xiξ drift away from θ\thetaθ whenever the estimate is biased, and the correction pulls it back onto the measured position. We use the gains kc=15k_c = 15kc​=15, Dinj=2D_\text{inj} = 2Dinj​=2, kξ=5k_\xi = 5kξ​=5, taken unchanged from the PHAST configuration.

    What the controller is told, and what it must estimate

    Everything above is fixed by physics and design — no component is learned. The only quantity the controller does not have outright is q˙^\hat{\dot q}q˙​^​, and it is precisely there that the comparison against a model-free policy is decided. We evaluate two variants:

    • Full-state oracle. q˙^=p/I\hat{\dot q} = p/Iq˙​^​=p/I from the true momentum. Training-free, and an observability upper bound rather than an optimal controller — it marks how well this fixed control law can possibly do, not how well the task can be done.
    • q-only observer. q˙^\hat{\dot q}q˙​^​ is produced by a finite-difference + TCN observer over a sliding window of the last 25 position measurements, matching the observation the RL policy receives. This is the apples-to-apples peer; the observer is the sole trained component.

    One implementation note, since it is easy to get wrong: our environment wraps θ\thetaθ to [−π,π][-\pi,\pi][−π,π] and the target q⋆=πq^\star = \piq⋆=π sits on that discontinuity, so ξ\xiξ is integrated in wrapped error coordinates rather than absolute angle — otherwise both (ξ−q⋆)(\xi - q^\star)(ξ−q⋆) and (θ−ξ)(\theta - \xi)(θ−ξ) jump by 2π2\pi2π at the goal.

    What the guarantee covers

    With the interconnection intact, damping injection gives H˙cl≤0\dot H_{cl} \leq 0H˙cl​≤0, and the shaped potential has a minimum at upright provided kc>mgLk_c > mgLkc​>mgL — satisfied here, 15 against 9.81. Two things qualify that for what we actually run. The corrector kξ(θ−ξ)k_\xi(\theta - \xi)kξ​(θ−ξ) sits outside the conservative structure, so CCC is contracted rather than conserved and the textbook bound is not inherited unchanged. And no such argument is available under wind at all: the construction certifies behaviour against the deterministic vector field, while σ(p) dWt\sigma(p)\,dW_tσ(p)dWt​ injects energy the law has no term to anticipate. We therefore treat the structural prior as buying accuracy, not stability under noise.

    CT-SAC

    Continuous-time Soft Actor-Critic: model-free, trained from scratch on the windy plant with the same q-only window the Casimir observer gets. It is given no physics — the structural prior handed to the Casimir side must be recovered from experience, if at all.

    What makes it continuous-time rather than a discrete agent on a fine grid is that the critic target is built from a step of length Δt\Delta tΔt instead of a fixed per-tick discount, with γ\gammaγ replaced by e−βΔte^{-\beta\Delta t}e−βΔt and the temporal difference divided by Δt\Delta tΔt:

    Qtarget  =  r  +  E[Q~(s,a)]  +  e−βΔt E[Q~(s′,a′)]−E[Q~(s,a)]Δt.Q_\text{target} \;=\; r \;+\; \mathbb{E}[\tilde Q(s,a)] \;+\; \frac{e^{-\beta\Delta t}\,\mathbb{E}[\tilde Q(s',a')] - \mathbb{E}[\tilde Q(s,a)]}{\Delta t}.Qtarget​=r+E[Q~​(s,a)]+Δte−βΔtE[Q~​(s′,a′)]−E[Q~​(s,a)]​.

    Reward

    With φ=wrap⁡(θ−π)\varphi = \operatorname{wrap}(\theta - \pi)φ=wrap(θ−π) and ω=p/I\omega = p/Iω=p/I, the base reward penalises angle, velocity and torque:

    rv0  =  −(φ2  +  0.01 ω2  +  10−4u2).r_{\text{v0}} \;=\; -\big(\varphi^2 \;+\; 0.01\,\omega^2 \;+\; 10^{-4}u^2\big).rv0​=−(φ2+0.01ω2+10−4u2).

    This is enough to reach upright and not enough to stay there. Because the torque penalty is paid every step while the angle penalty near upright is second-order, the policy settles at a steady-state offset just outside the target ball — under-actuating against gravity is cheaper than holding. Adding a per-step bonus for being inside the ball removes that trade-off:

    rv1  =  rv0  +  b 1 ⁣[φ2+ω2<ϵ],ϵ=0.1,    b=1.r_{\text{v1}} \;=\; r_{\text{v0}} \;+\; b\,\mathbb{1}\!\left[\sqrt{\varphi^2 + \omega^2} < \epsilon\right], \qquad \epsilon = 0.1,\;\; b = 1 .rv1​=rv0​+b1[φ2+ω2​<ϵ],ϵ=0.1,b=1.
    Disclosure

    The bonus uses the same ϵ\epsilonϵ and the same phase distance as the evaluation's success criterion, so CT-SAC is trained directly against the metric it is later scored on. The Casimir controller has no such alignment — it optimises nothing. This is a real asymmetry and it is most of why the success column comes out the way it does; the effort and final-error columns are the ones not affected by it.

    Configuration: MLP actor and critic [400,300][400, 300][400,300] with ReLU, two critics, β\betaβ-discount 0.980.980.98, τ=0.02\tau = 0.02τ=0.02, learning rate 7.3×10−47.3\times10^{-4}7.3×10−4, batch 256, replay buffer 3×1053\times10^{5}3×105, learning starts at 10410^4104 steps, automatic entropy temperature. Trained 1M steps per seed on q-only observations with a 25-frame window and torque capped at ±20\pm 20±20.

    Metrics

    Both controllers are scored by the same code, on the same rollouts. Writing φ=wrap⁡(θ−π)\varphi = \operatorname{wrap}(\theta - \pi)φ=wrap(θ−π) and ω=p/I\omega = p/Iω=p/I:

    • Final error. Phase distance to upright at the last step, φT2+ωT2\sqrt{\varphi_T^2 + \omega_T^2}φT2​+ωT2​​.
    • Success (sustained hold). Reached the ϵ=0.1\epsilon = 0.1ϵ=0.1 ball and stayed inside it for the final 50 steps — touching the target does not count.
    • Control effort. ∫u2 dt\textstyle\int u^2\,dt∫u2dt, accumulated over the episode.

    — worth one sentence on why sustained-hold rather than touch-once, since it is the choice that makes the wind results come out the way they do.

    Effort is ∫u2 dt\textstyle\int u^2\,dt∫u2dt. Emphasised cells mark the better value on that column. Every row is 20 evaluation episodes; the CT-SAC rows are three independently trained seeds and the mean row averages them, while the oracle is deterministic given the plant and has no training seed to vary.

    The learned policy wins the metric it was trained against and the oracle wins the two it was designed for. CT-SAC sustains upright in 93% of episodes against the oracle's 65%, but spends roughly 6.5× the control effort (64.0 vs 9.8) to do it, and the oracle still lands closer to true upright (0.040 vs 0.063 rad).

    It is worth being clear about why the full-state controller loses on success, since that looks backwards. The oracle is an observability upper bound, not an optimality one: it is a fixed energy-shaping law with gains carried over unchanged, so knowing ppp exactly removes any estimation error but does nothing about disturbance rejection. Its light fixed damping lets gusts knock it across the ϵ\epsilonϵ-ball boundary, which the sustained-hold criterion counts as failure even though the trajectory stays close. CT-SAC optimises a holding bonus that is a direct proxy for that criterion, on this exact plant, for a million steps — and pays for the difference in torque.

    The honest caveat is that the oracle is not the fair peer for a q-only policy. The apples-to-apples comparison is the q-only Casimir observer variant, which should do worse than the numbers above; until that row exists this table brackets the model-based side rather than pinning it down.

    Phase maps

    Where each controller actually settles

    Success rates say whether a controller held; they do not say where it went. Rolling both from the same grid of initial conditions and plotting where the orbits end separates two failures a table reports identically — settling at the wrong point, and settling nowhere. — then the finding: which controller homes to true upright and which parks at an offset. This is the figure the comparison rests on, so it is worth teaching the reader how to read it.

    — one paragraph on the mechanism. Both panels should use the same axes and the same wind level as the table above, or say so if they do not.

    Limitations

    What this does not show

    • The fair peer is missing. The Casimir side is represented by a full-state oracle. The q-only observer variant — the one matched to CT-SAC's observation — is not yet in the table.
    • Seed support is thin. Three CT-SAC seeds at one wind level; the sweep cells are unfilled. Both methods have been unreliable seed-to-seed in earlier work, so single-seed numbers here should not be read as trends.
    • Uniform sampling only. Everything runs at fixed Δt\Delta tΔt, so CT-SAC's Δt\Delta tΔt-aware updates — the thing that makes it continuous-time — are never exercised. — and one more you know of.
